title: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in perception.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Most of them, for example, recognize repetition, and some also recognize nesting. But almost none recognize anything more complex.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis” (from p. 632), p. 633. Scope: human perception and standard methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-24: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.28

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing benchmark results and method documentation could test restricted method classes. No comprehensive public census spans human perception and all practical mathematical, statistical, and computational analyses, and broad conclusions would depend heavily on taxonomy choices.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define a representative inventory of deployed perceptual and analytical methods, then classify the structural regularities each can detect under standardized benchmarks. The claim is supported only if nearly all methods detect repetition or nesting but systematically fail on agreed higher-order structures.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The quantifiers 'essentially all' and 'almost nothing more complex' lack fixed boundaries.

Method selection and the definition of higher-order regularity are contestable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.25
discriminating power: 0.25
data adequacy: 0.15
data existence: 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison is meaningful once recognition is tied to recovery of a known generator, and public libraries document the methods one would test. No existing catalog already classifies those methods by the Wolfram hierarchy of repetition, nesting, and beyond, so the test covers a curated subset rather than every method in use. Human perception and the phrase almost nothing more complex remain judgment calls, which keeps the outcome from deciding the claim at its stated scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a catalog of methods in routine scientific use and a test suite of sequences with known generators (periodic, nested substitution, and non-nested such as a cellular automaton). A method counts as recognizing a class if it recovers that generator under a pre-registered criterion. The claim is challenged if many practical methods recover non-nested generators, and supported only if almost all stop at repetition or nesting.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
What counts as practical use, as recognizing a pattern, and as more complex than nesting can be drawn in several incompatible ways.

A failed test shows only that a particular procedure missed a regularity, not that no practical method could detect it.

operationalizability: 0.45
data existence: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.4
analysis feasibility: 0.5
